One of my buddies was over Saturday night and mentioned this pedal. I found this demo and decided I might need one.

Anyone have any experience with them?

Haven’t used the Big Sky, but I’ve owned 2 blueSky’s in the past (sold, instant regret, bought, sold again a few years ago because I couldn’t justify owning both a blueSky and a Flint while out of a job and not actively performing).

It shines at very wet settings. Used it on a bunch of prog, post-rock, and soundtracky type recordings. The plate verb is great for swells. Ran vocals, synths through it too. Didn’t like the shimmer though.

I’d recommend a blueSky if you need to make a lot of wet noises. Can’t recommend a BigSky unless you have cash to blow and need the multiple presets… always more fun to tweak the knobs live IMO. But if you’re a more typical songwriter, you’re probably better off getting a much cheaper spring/plate reverb for gigs.

I'm sure I'd use it just like all of my other gear: set it and forget it. I generally use a pretty wet sound. About the only thing I fiddle with during a gig is my volume pedal and my delay when I'm setting the tempo. Presets on a pedal like that sure would be nice.

I mean, soundwise, the blueSky (and thus the BigSky) are definitely my favourite reverb pedals ever, and I’ve used a lot. I just can’t see paying 480 USD for the Big one. I’d buy an EHX Cathedral, TC Nova Reverb, and a vintage Boss RV-2 and have money left over for a nice dinner.

I took a peek at your SoundCloud btw. I think a Neunaber WET with an expression pedal could be more useful for you, if you want to be able to adjust the mix and don’t really need drastically different presets (like going from spring to shimmer between songs). Not to mention they sound amazing.

Hi new to this sub here and I have question for my fellow anarchists on this sub. Do you want the elimination of the state or the elimination of authority? What I mean by this is do you believe that the idea of the state could exist if it worked through a direct democratic system where the people could effect and change something at anytime.

Personally I want the elimination of Authority but what about you?
A question for all anarchist on this board.

I want the elimination of the state. As for "authority", it depends what you mean.

In his book, "The Problem of Political Authority: An Examination of the Right to Coerce and the Duty to Obey," Michael Huemer used the term "political authority" to mean the supposed right of governments to do do things that most people would see as unjust if done by anyone else but governments. He concludes, and I agree, that this kind of authority does not exist and that governments should be abolished.

"Authority" can also mean non-coerced deference due to respect for (real or imagined) superior knowledge or wisdom. I don't see how anyone could object to this kind of authority.

Thirdly, "authority" could mean the right to exclude other people by force from one's own property. Some anarchists deny that this right exists. I think that their position is absurd and morally repugnant. In the absence of respect for property rights, we would have the rule of pure brute force. For me, the state is immoral and intolerable precisely because it necessarily violates property rights.

As for democracy (direct or otherwise), it's fine for voluntary organizations that want to operate that way, but a democratic state is not inherently better than an autocratic one. The fundamental problem with the state is that it imposes itself on people against their will. The oppression of a minority, by a majority, is no better than the oppression of a majority, by a minority. Simply being in the majority confers no moral rights whatever.

It depends on how you define the state. Early anarchists like Mikhail Bakunin considered the state to be a network of repressive institutions that exercised intrusive authority over people. Without intrusive authority, there was no state.

Intrusiveness is the key -- the state depends on coercive authority. Natural authority, the kind where people defer to each other in an organic way (as you would to your doctor), is fine. The state is synonymous with intrusive authority.

The work of administrating communities and the existence of institutions isn't the same thing as having a state. Think of the state as a family of institutions which have the power to control you whereas anarchism would be a society where institutions are powerless to assert control over people who aren't asserting control over others.

There'd still be limited cases of coercion (forcing state-builders to leave communities, managing violent criminals, etc), but there'd be no overarching complex of repressive institutions.

How an anarchist society might operate is a question that doesn't need a single answer. I'm a partisan of panarchism, a framework that advocates political experimentation. I'm wary of direct democracy because of its despotic tendencies, but there's no reason why people shouldn't be allowed to try their hand at it. We need to roll up our sleeves and try a thousand different things. I don't think we'll ever find The One True Way to liberty, and anyone who offers up one-size-fits-all political solutions should probably be ignored.

Think of it as iterative anarchism: let people build a bunch of versions (the Kurdish are experimenting with municipal libertarianism over in Rojava right now), and then we'll see what sticks.

One of Bakunin's common attacks against Marx was that he was procrustean -- he tried to fit the world into a predetermined framework, and when the world didn't match up with his ideas, instead of ditching his framework, he'd favor the theory in his head over the facts on the ground.

The most important thing we can do is take action in the here and now and experiment.

Put differently: there's a substantial difference between how you imagine sex with a new partner will be and what having sex with them actually feels like. In the same way, ideas of what anarchism will be like in practice will never match up to the actualities of real-life anarchism, because anarchism involves coordinating action with other people -- people who possess agency and free will, and are damn near impossible to predict.

TLDR: I want to experiment, because I don't claim to know what liberty will look like in practice, and it'd be a mistake to make any hard rules over how it should play out.
